newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New refinery may help free up S.Africa gold market.
newsitem.headline: New refinery may help free up S.Africa gold market.

text.p: South Africa could launch its own bullion market once the Reserve Bank lifts foreign exchange controls and grants mines the right to market all their own gold, said Mike Brown, research head of broker Frankel Pollak.
Currently all mines have to sell their gold to the Reserve Bank, which markets it or holds the metal or any dollar proceeds as reserves, controlling the flow of foreign exchange.
All mines refine their gold at the Rand Refinery -- the world's biggest -- which is collectively owned by the industry.

But a revolutionary move announced by Harmony Gold Mining Co Ltd on Thursday may have started the reform ball rolling. Harmony is to set up its own refinery and has applied for permission to market its own gold internationally.
"If exchange controls go, then as part of the whole process we could decide to set up a gold market in South Africa," Brown told Reuters.
"Instead of having to sell everything through London and Zurich, we could say you come to us...But exchange controls would have to be removed."

While economists argue abolition of forex controls is vital, authorities' hands are tied by low official gold and forex reserves which, despite a slight improvement last month, remain precarious at just 10.28 million rand.

Harmony managing director Bernard Swanepoel believes the authorities will grant the mine permission to market its own gold. "We are very optimistic that we would actually be granted permission to sell our own gold. Towards the end of July we had a meeting with the minister of trade and industry (Alec Erwin) who was fairly excited about the project and lent his full and total support," Swanepoel said.
Brown said that if permission were granted to one mine, permission would have to be granted to the whole industry.

Brown said that gold marketing was being discussed by the government and Reserve Bank with the mining industry as part of the whole foreign exchange control reform process, which would allow proceeds from exports to flow freely through the market.

"The Reserve Bank now holds those dollars from gold sales, so the market is always short of the dollar proceeds and has to go to the Bank to get those dollars. This helps the Bank to regulate the forex market. If that goes, then it reduces that particular control that the Reserve Bank holds," Brown said.
In a free market, if the Reserve Bank wanted to build up its gold reserves it would need to buy gold from the industry on the open market and offer a better price, he said.

The prime motivation for the new refinery, however, is to save costs. Harmony said the cost of establishing the plant and acquiring new technology would be 3.3 million rand, which is less than the annual savings it expects to achieve by smelting and refining its own gold.

Work on the refinery will start immediately and is scheduled for completion in the third quarter of 1997. The refinery has been designed to produce two tonnes of 99.99 percent pure gold per month -- sufficient to process Harmony's total gold output.
